newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposition hopes to increase vote share.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposition hopes to increase vote share.

text.p: Singapore's main opposition Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) expects to increase its share of the vote in the country's next general election and win more seats, SDP Secretary-General Chee Soon Juan said on Wednesday.

Chee told Reuters the SDP, which currently holds three of the four opposition seats in Singapore's 81-seat parliament, had an uphill task campaigning in a society heavily dominated by the ruling People's Action Party (PAP).
But he said he thought the SDP's support had risen since the last general election in September 1991.

"Opinion polls are not carried out here, but...everyone keeps saying the government's share of the vote will fall again. I think it will," Chee said in an interview. "I'm really hoping we can improve our numbers to about 10 opposition MPs."

Chee said the SDP was hoping it could agree a "by-election strategy" with the other small opposition parties under which they would not contest a majority of parliament seats at the general elections, which must be held by April 1997.

A by-election is a vote in one or a small number of parliamentary seats. Because the outcome of a by-election rarely changes control of the government, voting patterns tend to be more volatile and often favour opposition parties.
Chee said such a strategy would mean automatically re-electing the PAP, but it would also allow oppostion parties to concentrate their resources in a few constituencies.

The SDP and rival Workers Party used a similar tactic at the 1991 general election, contesting 40 out of 81 seats. On that occasion, the opposition vote rose to a high of 39 percent, from under 37 percent in 1988 and around 24 percent in 1980.

"At the general election we are hoping to field candidates in less than 50 percent of the seats so that Singaporeans will not be afraid to cast their votes for us, knowing the PAP will become the government," Chee said.
"We would probably field not less than 10 to 15 candidates, hoping the rest of the opposition parties will also field a few," he said, adding, "We are working towards a deal."
The PAP has dominated Singapore since its first polls for a fully elected self-government under the British in 1959.

Under Lee Kuan Yew, prime minister from 1959 to 1990, the PAP government steered the island through independence in 1965 and transformed it from a port heavily dependent on colonial trade to one of the biggest financial markets in the world.

But Chee said many Singaporeans now thought the strong government control that may have been necessary during the country's early rapid development was no longer appropriate in a nation ranked among the world's richest.
Singapore's average per capita income was US$22,400 last year, the ninth highest in the world.

Chee said he thought the opposition's total share of the vote might only rise slightly but said the number of opposition members of parliament (MPs) could increase if the vote was concentrated in a few areas.

"In terms of percentage I think it is going to remain at about 40:60...but translated into the number of seats, I think there is a lot of (potential) improvement in that area," he said. "If we can actually tip over that 50 percent mark in a few more areas, we can get more seats."
Chee said he thought Singapore's next general election would probably be held in December, after the World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting is held in Singapore December 9-13.
Under Singapore's constitution, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong may call an election at any time before April 1997.
Goh said in August there were four possibilities for the elections -- in November, December, February and March.
